chapter: Boyhood in Webster Groves and early roadhouse work
title: Learning jazz at twelve; Langford's leeway
summary: Thomas had no jazz experience, but four years of lessons and records of Louis Armstrong helped. Langford let the band swing a Sousa march and played at Fallon Park.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: But where would you have heard them?
Well, I'm jumping the gun, Stan. I've heard them on the boats. But, now they were popular through that whole ...
Yeah but what I meant was when you started in that road house, presumably you were going to be sort of playing jazz of a kind, now you haven't had much experience of this before.
But you had a good enough ear to make it with them?
Well, they thought so and I thought so, too.
Well, I don't know. When you're 12 years old, had four years of lessons and I'd heard about Charlie Creath (?) and I'd listened to Louis Armstrong, whom I admired very much and I had a chance to ...
But, you'd heard him on records?

Records, yeah, up to that time. And, Mr. Langford, of course, was always an inspiration because of the things, not on popular tunes but he -- I'll tell you what he was. He was the kind of man who would get in this way, he'd play a march, say, like a Sousa march. He would give in to the ideas we might have. He say, well, let's all do it that way. Let's do it this way. Let's swing it, you know. He'd let us go.
But I mean Langford was not in any sense a jazz musician.
He was strictly sort of legitimate.
Oh, yeah but he had a way with kids. He'd give us a little leeway that we needed.

Yeah. He'd give us our freedom. We'd go down to (?) a place called Old Fallon Park in St. Louis. And, in fact, my brother took me down there the other day and my niece lives park right across from the ap and I was very much surprised. I know play at this park. We used to go down and paint the little band know shindigs there, you kew.
